title: Unveiling Mucorales infections: A cutting-edge longitudinal imaging approach for real-time infection and host-response monitoring in  Galleria mellonella  and mouse models

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Unveiling Mucorales infections: A cutting-edge longitudinal imaging approach for real-time infection and host-response monitoring in  Galleria mellonella  and mouse models》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · s0001-p1】Mucormycosis, caused by fungi of the Mucorales order, manifests in various clinical forms, including devastating pulmonary and rhino-orbital-cerebral infections. These often require surgical intervention involving the removal of facial and bone tissue, leading to profound life-changing morbidities and high mortality rates [1–6]. The most common genera associated with human disease are Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia and Rhizomucor [1,7]. The incidence of Mucorales infections is rising, with an estimated mean annual occurrence of 211,000 cases and mortality in untreated invasive fungal disease remains close to 100% [1,8,9]. This is concerning not only for immunocompromised populations such as hematologic and solid organ transplant patients, but also for other at-risk groups, including patients with diabetes mellitus or iron anomalies [5] which are more strongly linked to mucormycosis than to other invasive fungal diseases (IFD). Moreover, mucormycosis has been documented in multiple cases among influenza and COVID-19 patients, likely related to virus-host responses and corticosteroid therapies, with reported mortality rates ranging from 15% to 90% [10–12]. It also represents one of the few invasive fungal infections that can affect immunocompetent individuals, particularly in the context of severe burns, traumatic injuries, or combat wounds [13–15].

【Introduction · s0001-p2】Overall, Mucorales fungi are generally resistant to most antifungal agents, resulting in a markedly limited therapeutic arsenal compared to other fungal pathogens. Available treatment options are restricted mainly to liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, and isavuconazole [2,16]. Furthermore, treatment with the available antifungals is limited by renal toxicity, prolonged and costly regimens, challenges with routes of administration, and significant drug–drug interactions [17]. The unacceptably high mortality rates associated with mucormycosis reflect not only the aggressive nature of the infection and the limitations of current antifungals but also highlight the inability of the immune system to effectively prevent or clear the infection. The reported alarming outcomes underscore the urgent need for a better understanding of mucormycosis host–pathogen interactions and the development of novel therapeutic and prophylactic strategies. As such, the World Health Organization has recognized mucormycosis infections as a global threat and the urgency of these priorities, calling for increased awareness and collaborative interdisciplinary efforts (One Health approach) to mitigate the emergence of the disease and development of preventive-therapeutic strategies [18].

【Introduction · s0001-p4】Therefore, there is a critical need for innovative disease models, methodologies and analytical readouts to overcome current limitations and enable longitudinal tracking of disease progression and host–pathogen interactions over time, particularly in models that simulate mucormycosis-predisposing conditions in patients. Noninvasive modalities, such as bioluminescence (BL) or micro-CT imaging, enable longitudinal monitoring of individual animals, providing real-time insights into fungal burden kinetics and host-induced disease development, respectively. These approaches allow for repeated assessments at multiple time points, thereby increasing sensitivity and enhancing our understanding of the disease over time. Such imaging modalities and strategies have been successfully applied in studying other fungi, including Aspergillus fumigatus and Cryptococcus neoformans [21–23]. Furthermore, by preventing the need to sacrifice animals at different time points, these approaches align with the principles of the 3Rs (Reduction, Replacement and Refinement) in promoting ethically humane animal research [21,23–28].

sections.text:

【Generation of strains · s0002-s2001-p2】First, a synthetic codon-optimized version of the firefly (Photinus pyralis) luciferase gene (without peroxisomal target sequence) was generated by back-translating the amino acid sequence into DNA sequence (http://genomes.urv.es/OPTIMIZER/), applying the Mucor lusitanicus codon usage table. Codon usage frequencies for M. circinelloides f. lusitanicus were obtained from the Codon Usage Database (NCBI-GenBank Release; kazusa.or.jp; http://www.kazusa.or.jp/codon/cgibin/showcodon.cgi?species=29924&aa=4&style=N) [32]. The codon-optimized luciferase sequence, flanked by XhoI and SacII restriction sites, was synthesized by GeneArt Gene Synthesis Service (Thermofisher, Germany) and subcloned into the standard vector pMAT, yielding the plasmid pMAT_luc_opt. To replicate higher light emission achieved in previous constructs [27], we generated plasmids containing the respective luciferase sequence under the control of either zinc permease zrt1 (ID 1,540,454; Mucor lusitanicus CBS277.49 vs 3; http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/Mucci3/Mucci3.home.html) [33] or the histone 3, his3 (ID 157,320, Mucor lusitanicus CBS277.49 vs 2; http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/Mucci2/Mucci2.home.html) [34] promoter and a functional leuA gene as selective marker, integrated in carRP (Figure S1). Targeted integration of the whole construct in the Mucor carRP gene was aimed to achieve easier identification of positive clones, as positive clones formed white colonies, due to disturbance of carotene biosynthesis, while those without integration had a yellow phenotype. As previously, strain R7B (leuA-) was used as the recipient strain. Generation of protoplasts and the transformation procedure were performed by electroporation as described before [27]. Positive transformants (white colonies) were repeatedly transferred to fresh selective agar plates (3–4 cycles) to obtain homokaryons, tested for light emission by luminometer, and checked by colony PCR. Therefore, site-specific integration of the fragment containing leuA, respective promoter and luciferase, was checked using a primer set flanking the integration site (carRP-ExtF1: 5´GGGCACATTGACGTAGAAGG, binding upstream of 5´ region and carp-ExtR1: 5´GCTGTTGCTGTGCTAACATCAT, binding downstream of 3´ region). PCR products were visualized by electrophoresis on a 0.8 % agarose gel. Integration was identified by a size shift of the PCR product from 4.6kb in the parental strain (R7B) and 9.6kb in the positive transformants (Figure S2). Briefly, 2 µg of DNA was digested overnight with 20 units of NcoI at 37°C, separated on a 0.8% agarose gel, transferred to nylon membrane, and hybridized with a DIG-labeled probe targeting the luciferase coding sequence.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Unveiling Mucorales infections: A cutting-edge longitudinal imaging approach for real-time infection and host-response monitoring in  Galleria mellonella  and mouse models》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · f0001】Figure 1. Light emission of individual luciferase-expressing strains in dependence of luciferin concentration A) and over a 30 min timeframe B). Strains were grown in YNB medium inoculated with 1 × 105 spores/ml of spores from the respective strains, light emission was induced by the addition of D-luciferin after 24 h by injectors and light was detected by Varioscan Lux (Thermo Fischer Scientific) microplate reader using a kinetic protocol with one reading every minute and dispensing D-luciferin at time point 2. Relative light units (RLUs) represent the average of three independent measurements, in total, 18 wells per sample, normalized to biomass (OD620 nm). A) Light emission values measured immediately after the addition of luciferin; error bars indicate standard deviation. B) shows kinetic curve of each strain confronted with 0.5 µM of D-luciferin. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test. Statistical evaluation is shown only for the comparison of luciferin concentration in dependence on codon usage.

【Figure 2. · f0002】Figure 2. In vivo bioluminescence reveals promoter-dependent differences among codon-optimized M. lusitanicus strains. Comparative bioluminescence of G. mellonella larvae infected with 1 × 106 spores of codon-optimized M. lusitanicus strains 48 h post-infection. A) Representative images of infected larvae following injection of 60 µl of 10 mM D-luciferin (IVIS Spectrum in vivo Imaging System, PerkinElmer). B) Quantification of bioluminescent signals (radiance, p/sec/cm2) using grid regions of interest (ROI) function. Values were normalized by subtracting the average signal from the control larvae (1 = uninfected larvae, 2 = uninfected but luciferin-injected larvae). The experiment was done in triplicate.

【Figure 3. · f0003】Figure 3. Novel bioluminescent M. lusitanicus strains enable real-time monitoring of mucormycosis infection in G. mellonella. G. mellonella larvae were infected with M. lusitanicus AII or CII bioluminescent (BL) strains to compare BL signal emission and infection progression. Inoculum doses ranging from 1 × 103 to 1 × 106 spores were used to assess inoculum-dependent dynamics (1 × 103 shown in Figure S7A–C). A, D) Longitudinal health scores (Table 2) provided an index of infection severity (% decrease). B, E) survival curves of larvae post-infection, highlighting mortality rates over time according to inoculum. C, F) Quantitative analysis of light emission signals from larvae (total flux) over time and G) representative BLI images comparison from each experimental bioluminescent strain-group (1 × 106 inoculum; n = 6). Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test, assessing differences between groups over time (lateral comparisons on legends) and relative to sham-infected per time point (significance markers above curves; color denotes the group exhibiting significant differences). Longitudinal data were evaluated on day 3. Survival data were analyzed using a log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Statistical significance is indicated as p ≤ *p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, ****p ≤ 0.0001.
